findings.title: Async legacy write uses the request ctx, which is cancelled when the request returns
findings.body: The goroutines launched in Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection derive their context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause. When the HTTP request finishes, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy write is aborted almost immediately after the response is sent. The 'asynchronous safe measure' write will frequently fail silently (only logged/metric'd), leaving legacy out of sync. The background goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) plus the timeout.

findings.title: Create passes the same obj to legacy asynchronously after storage may have mutated it
findings.body: The goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the same obj and options that were just passed to Storage.Create, concurrently with the returned object being used by the caller. Storage Create/Update implementations can mutate the object (e.g. set ResourceVersion, UID, generated name), so the legacy write races with those mutations (data race detected by -race) and may write different content than what was stored in unified storage.

findings.title: Update reuses objInfo for legacy after storage consumed it
findings.body: objInfo is an UpdatedObjectInfo whose UpdatedObject is typically called by Storage.Update, and the same objInfo is then passed to the async legacy Update. The legacy update will run the transform again against the current stored state of legacy (or a different old object), and it may race with the storage call that is still using objInfo. The previous implementation carefully wrapped the storage result for the legacy write; that was removed, so legacy may get a different object than what was written to unified storage.

findings.title: Update goroutine leaks the context cancel on a path that never calls cancel promptly
findings.body: In Update, the context.WithTimeoutCause is created in the goroutine, but cancel is deferred after the timer is set and it is fine; however the cancel is only called after Legacy.Update returns. The ctx variable is shadowed correctly, but the timeout starts before startLegacy is measured; minor, though combined with the request ctx cancellation the goroutine has no independent lifetime control.

findings.title: Delete storage duration metric records the object name as the kind label
findings.body: In Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with `name` in the kind position instead of options.Kind, so the metric label cardinality explodes per object name and the kind dimension is wrong, unlike every other method.

findings.title: Update error path records a legacy metric for a storage failure
findings.body: When Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage failures are counted as legacy errors and storage error metrics are never incremented for update.

findings.title: DeleteCollection async legacy duration is recorded with the storage metric
findings.body: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its outcome with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, corrupting storage vs legacy metrics.

findings.title: Delete attaches the parent logger instead of the scoped log
findings.body: ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) in Delete discards the log with name/kind/method values that was just built, so downstream logs lose context. Inconsistent with other methods.

findings.title: options.Kind dereferenced for nil-safe access and CreateOptions has no Kind field used reliably
findings.body: log uses options.Kind on *metav1.CreateOptions etc.; these option types' Kind is set only via TypeMeta and is often empty, so the logs/metrics label is frequently blank. Mode 3 metrics labels depend on this.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy write happens
findings.body: The tests set up legacy mock expectations but never assert they were called, and the goroutine can race with test teardown. Failures in the legacy write (the core of mode 3 behavior) are untested; the Update failure test has no legacy expectation at all.

findings.title: New mode 3 integration cases are not tied to legacy consistency checks
findings.body: The new mode 3 cases run the same doPlaylistTests, which asserts only unified-storage results; since legacy writes are asynchronous and not awaited, the tests cannot detect the legacy write being lost, so the added coverage does not validate the feature.
